doc.title: Henry Johnson interviewed by Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 30, 1995

chapter: Learning from masters and guitar ideas
title: Phrasing like a wind player, transcribed solos and wrong notes
summary: On breathing into phrases, why transcribed solos miss interaction, no wrong note if followed by a right one, and McCoy and Herbie Hancock on tension and release.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Do you find yourself when you solo when you play your lines, do you find yourself phrasing like a wind player?

Yeah. Yeah, I think because if you don’t everything ends up sounding like an exercise. You have to breathe life into the phrase by actually putting air into it and breathing with it. And that’s what a lot of the guys that are coming out of schools now, they don’t realize, they work with a lot of transcribed solos. But when you look at a solo on a piece of paper without actually listening to it being done, you don’t really correlate why a guy did this, you know? You see a weird note on there and you think oh, that’s just his idea. He did that weird note because of something that the piano player played or something the drummer played or the bass player played. It was the interaction, and that didn’t come out on the transcribed solo. © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

You know I was trans — not transcribing but looking at a transcribed solo, one of Dizzy’s solos. And I was looking at the chord changes, and then I was looking at the notes. And I said there are so many wrong notes on there. I said there’s more wrong notes than there is right notes. If you look at it stagnantly on paper, there’s a ton of wrong notes. But if you listen to it at speed it’s exciting because he can play with such authority, that he can take all them wrong notes and sell them to you.
Well see the thing is, there is no wrong note if it’s followed by a right one.
Or if it’s put in context.

Yeah because it’s only a way of getting there. What you’re looking at is the end result, and you might find a bunch of different ways to get there, and a bunch of different roads, but they all end up at the same spot. And I think that the ways that people get there is their own, that’s their identification. Say like McCoy has a different way if you’re just taking a regular two five, McCoy has a different way of getting there; Herbie Hancock has a different way of getting there, but that way of getting there that’s the excitement that makes them their own person. We can look at a Basie two five. A lot of guys approaching two five as okay, we’ll play on the minor seventh chord, then we’ll play on the seventh chord, then we’ll play on the major chord. But Herbie has a technique of playing on the five, which, and I heard this with McCoy first. They’re playing on the five chord and then they’ll go up and play on the sharp five chord and come back down. Well Herbie plays on the five, goes up to the sharp five, and extends it and stays on there until the last half of the beat of the four, and he hangs over. So after the one, the downbeat of the next bar of the one chord, he comes in after and relieves the tension. So when I was studying McCoy and listening to a lot of McCoy’s, it’s about tension and release. You know you keep building up tension after tension until you find, you finally get release.
Or build tension in such a way that you have the option to either fulfill or disguise.
